Moving from the safe enclosure of early beginnings to the inevitable compulsion to shed one’s skin, the work serves as an ode to blooming out of step, in one's own authentic hues. By leaving behind inherited expectations to embrace the painful, miraculous nature of metamorphosis, the series stands as a vital reminder that to truly inhabit the world is, at its bravest, a lifelong act of self-transformation. Watch Full Video Here

EL TIGRE ME PERSIGUE (The Tiger Pursues Me)

This photograph is part of the series ‘EL TIGRE ME PERSIGUE (The Tiger Pursues Me)’. Created by Alcira Angelo, the project is an intimate photographic odyssey that explores self-discovery through the emotional and psychological terrain of duelo—a concept evoking both inner struggle and the reckoning that follows loss. The work unfolds as a visual dialogue with the self and others, constructing a quiet yet insistent collective portrait of grief and resilience.

This photograph is part of the series ‘My friend, Whisky’. The project chronicles the eight-year creative bond between photographer Fee-Gloria Grönemeyer and her muse and collaborator, Whisky Boonjongrux. Having developed multiple photographic dialogues together that consistently push both toward new creative horizons, the series stands as an intimate reflection on artistic trust, mutual growth, and the quiet courage required to be wholly oneself.

This photograph is part of the series ‘UNCOOL’. A study in visibility, embodiment, and representation, the project brings together twenty-seven portraits of individuals with disabilities and visible physical differences. Informed by the artist’s lived experience as a wheelchair user, the work examines how bodies are perceived, categorized, and normalized through imagery, critically questioning which bodies are granted visibility, under what conditions, and through which prevailing visual conventions.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Matriphagie’. The project investigates how societal structures transmit and internalize prescribed norms of femininity from an early age. Structured around interviews and encounters with young girls aged four to eleven, the work uses their testimonies—balancing between learned clichés and instinctive transgressions—to ground a visual inquiry into the ambivalences, tensions, and shifting definitions of the feminine.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Look at me like you love me’. Informed by the artist’s identity as a queer, nonbinary individual, the work explores the complexities of personhood, desire, intimacy, and family. Motivated by an existential search for self-understanding and human connection, the project centers on the radical necessity of living authentically and the mutual power of seeing and being seen, using intimate storytelling to invite viewers into deep reflection on their own identities and relationships.

This photograph is part of the series ‘t-fags’. Bringing together photographs and interviews with trans men, transmasculine, and non-binary people who identify with the reclaimed term ‘fag’, the project explores masculinities that openly embrace femininity and gender expansiveness. By challenging heteronormative expectations around gender transition, the work documents a community asserting radical self-definition. Created between 2022 and 2025, the series was self-published as a limited-edition artist book in 2026, serving as a vital archive of contemporary queer identity.

This photograph is part of the series ‘People’. Built on friendship, attraction, and creative collaboration, this ongoing portrait project actively reclaims who is pictured as desirable and who holds the authority behind the lens. Centering disabled subjects through the perspective of a gay, disabled photographer, the work employs nudity, fashion, and playful experimentation to capture beauty infused with sexual confidence, humor, and unfiltered desire.

This photograph is part of the series ‘I Love My Friends But They Are Killing Me’. The project examines contemporary beauty standards and their psychological toll through portraits of young Indian women navigating micro-celebrity—influencers, reality television figures, and aspiring actors pictured inside their private bedrooms and homes. Shot primarily on 35mm film with harsh direct flash and framed by episodic, reality-TV-style text, the work strikes a deliberate tension between cultural critique, intimate vulnerability, and biting absurdity.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Cut from the Street’. The project examines hair as a medium of self-expression, identity, and resistance among young men across north and central Chennai. Through portraits and interviews, the work interrogates how caste, class, skin tone, and urban geography dictate who is granted social legitimacy and visibility. Highlighting how identical aesthetics celebrated as fashion on privileged bodies are condemned as “indecent” or suspicious on others, the series reveals everyday styling as an act of defiance—a vital claim to presence and the right to be seen.

This photograph is part of the series ‘TOPS’. Extending the world of the companion short film, the work gathers intimate moments captured before, during, and after production to trace the profound physical and emotional journey of top surgery. Through quiet, behind-the-scenes glimpses, the collection documents the urgency of gender-affirming care, the essential networks of community support that sustain it, and the deep vulnerability that shapes the path toward embodied self-realization.

The Water Bring We, The Water Wanna Take We Back

This photograph is part of the series 'The Water Bring We, The Water Wanna Take We Back', a project that explores the Gullah Geechee corridor as a landscape of memory, survival, and spiritual continuity. Drawing on a Gullah proverb and the Bakongo cosmogram, the project examines water as both rupture and return—marking histories of the Middle Passage while sustaining cultural resilience. Through photographs of the Low Country, the work considers how Geechee communities navigate displacement, climate change, and enduring ancestral presence.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Who’s Afraid of the Bad Wolf?’. Documenting the bedroom as the foundational universe of childhood, the work explores a space where solitude, play, and resilience are first tested, and where fantasy and reality seamlessly coexist. Centered on the intimate bedtime rituals invented by children to cultivate safety and ward off fear, the ongoing archive currently traces the private domestic worlds of eleven children across Piedmont, Italy.

This photograph is part of the series ‘An Anatomy of Fear’. Reflecting on fear as a collective condition shaped by uncertainty, instability and the accelerating pace of contemporary life, Alvaro Deprit explores the fragile territory between identity and transformation. Through images of unfinished clay and plaster sculptures, alongside the students who inhabit the art school where the work was made, he draws a parallel between bodies and forms in the process of becoming. Adolescence emerges as a particularly charged moment of this transition, when identity remains fluid and the boundaries between vulnerability and possibility are still being negotiated.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Thoughts, Feelings, Behaviour’. Begun in 2024, the project employs staged photography to interrogate narcissistic self-image, emotional isolation, and the alienating demands of the capitalist attention economy. Exploring the fraught boundary between self-sufficiency and raw vulnerability, the work navigates currents of desire, aggression, and melancholy. Through an experimental synthesis of body paint, collage, and sculptural props, the imagery blurs the lines between lens-based practice, painting, and tactile material experience.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Ọ Hụrụ M’—translating to “She Saw Me” in the artist’s native tongue, Igbo. Conceived as an intimate dialogue across her past, present, and future selves, this self-portrait project treats the camera lens as both a transformative portal and an unbound playground. Navigating life as a young Nigerian woman raised in the United States, the artist claims absolute authorship over her representation. Standing firmly as both creator and subject, she transforms self-imaging into a sovereign act of agency, radical ownership, and resistance against cultural erasure.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Rose Sarajevo: Girls from the East’. Weaving together portraits of young women, local architecture, and surrounding nature, the project traces the enduring scars of conflict across an urban landscape under quiet reconstruction—most visibly marked by the “Sarajevo Roses,” mortar damage filled with red resin to memorialize fallen lives. Guided by fragmented memories, the artist undertakes an intimate quest for the origins of her own identity, using photography as an act of personal and historical reconciliation, an attempt to mend and bridge the fractures of time.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Home Story’. Combining documentary and staged photography, the project unearths fragmented, visceral narratives within a space fundamentally promised as a sanctuary: the domestic home. Acknowledging the difficulty of articulating trauma into daily reality, the work interrogates how patriarchal structures isolate survivors of domestic violence into silenced, individualized tragedies. By confronting the quiet complicity of institutional secrecy, the imagery functions as an act of disclosure—insisting that giving voice to these hidden experiences dismantles the systemic machinery that thrives on their suppression.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Scarlet Spirit’. Grounded in the enduring legacy of the 1947 Partition of India, the project traces the artist’s familial migration through ancestral memory and oral histories gathered across Kolkata’s refugee colonies. Synthesizing contemporary portraits, archival material, and surreal visual metaphors, the work constructs a layered archive of displacement that interrogates severed roots, cultural erasure, and collective resilience. Created in resonance with the milestone commemorations of Partition, the series links generational trauma and the arduous labor of rebuilding to the broader, ongoing realities of global displacement today.

The Drying Leaves: A Domestic Cartography Initiative

This photograph is part of the series ‘The Drying Leaves : A Domestic Cartography Initiative’. Set beneath the ancestral neem tree of Suktara, the work adopts the seasonal descent of winter leaves as a poignant metaphor for the passage of time and human mortality. Through a three-dimensional visual approach that weaves together photography, family archives, and spoken histories, the initiative maps intimate domestic geographies to resist alienation and stave off the "third death"—the quiet disappearance that occurs when a person’s name is spoken for the very last time.

This video is part of the series ‘Everything I Am or Have Since Become’. Centering on the elemental nature of water as a metaphor for queer safety—at once life-giving sanctuary and volatile peril—the project weaves together collective oral histories, writings, and movement developed collaboratively with an all-queer cast and crew. Created by diasporic artists navigating New York City in resistance to systemic precarity, the work follows three figures across aquatic terrains in ritualistic choreography. Through sustained cycles of grief, repetition, and bodily rebirth, the series meditates on the search for refuge in hostile environments, embodying the fluid, precarious nature of both sanctuary and identity. Watch Full Video Here

This photograph is part of the project ‘Driving License’. Exploring an online subculture where people buy and sell photographs of other people’s faces to use as their own, Lean Lui examines the shifting boundaries between identity, ownership and authenticity in the digital age. Through a three-month investigation in which she actively participated in these transactions, Lui explores how a face can become a commodity, a disguise or a new identity altogether. The work questions what it means to be seen, and whether an image can stand in for a person who does not exist.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Mixed / Unmistakably You’. Created by Norwegian-Indian artist Dev Dhunsi, the project takes the artist’s own mixed heritage as an inquiry into the nuances of cultural and personal identity. In a society where language lacks a direct term for mixedness, the work pairs photography and text to articulate experiences that have long remained unnamed. Interrogating how belonging, visibility, and intimacy are mediated by race, gender, and desire, the series constructs a luminous visual vocabulary for self-definition beyond existing cultural lexicons.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Constructed Portrait’. In an era marked by frictionless image oversaturation, the project investigates the blurred boundaries between the tangible and the synthetic. Confronting the extractive reality of digital photography—where personal images are systematically harvested as training data for artificial intelligence—the artist restricts the source material strictly to their own intimate photo archive. By algorithmically synthesizing and deconstructing these personal traces into a self-portrait, the work deploys technology against itself, functioning simultaneously as an ethical data citation, a formal technical critique, and an enduring act of self-reflection.

This video is part of the series ‘Nox’. Drawing from Rio Nakada’s lived experiences of complex PTSD, dissociation, and Alice in Wonderland Syndrome, the work translates internal psychological instability into an embodied sensory environment. Through fractured memories, shifting architectures, mirrored reflections, and visceral bodily distortions, the imagery renders an otherwise invisible, disorienting mental landscape spatial and tangible. Selected for the 83rd Venice International Film Festival, the project functions as an intimate bridge between isolation and communion, inviting the viewer into a briefly shared architecture of altered perception. Watch Full Video Here

This photograph is part of the series ‘We Knew the World in Fragments of Color’. Reflecting on the personal journey of migration from Venezuela to the United States, the project explores the dislocating experience of diaspora, cultural belonging, and the fractured nature of memory. Through meticulous staged compositions and handcrafted wearable constructions, the work harnesses heightened chromatic symbolism to reconstruct a displaced home, transforming personal nostalgia into a vivid, allegorical visual language.

Meet the international jury of Brave New Visions: Creativity as Rebellion, bringing together artists, photographers, editors, curators, and creative voices from different disciplines and backgrounds. Together with the Vogue and Condé Nast Committee, comprising more than 100 editorial and creative professionals from across our global brands, these jurors have brought their individual perspectives and sensibilities to the selection process. Their participation reflects something fundamental to PhotoVogue's philosophy: there is no single authority on what makes an image meaningful, no universal definition of beauty, and no one way of seeing the world. It is through the encounter of different perspectives that new possibilities emerge.

Born in Addis Ababa in 1974, Aïda graduated from Howard University with a degree in Communications, majoring in Film. Her photography is in major collections including MoMA, the Smithsonian, and the RISD Museum. She’s received numerous awards, including the EU Prize in Bamako, the CRAF Award, and the Royal Photographic Society Award. Aïda co-curated the Nobel Peace Prize exhibition in 2019 and was a commissioned artist in 2020. A Canon ambassador and founder of Addis Foto Fest and Africa Foto Fair, she also leads Africa Print House and advocates for health, the environment, and photography across Africa.

Alex Consani is a model and actress who was named 2024 Model of the Year at the Fashion Awards in London, becoming the first transgender woman to receive the award. A face of Gucci and YSL Beauty, she has graced the digital cover of American Vogue and made history as one of the first transgender women to walk the Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show. Her acting credits include American Horror Story: 13 and A24’s upcoming film Peaked.

Curator, Founder & Artistic Director, Culture Art Society (CAS)

Awa Konaté is an independent curator, cultural strategist, and founder of Culture Art Society (CAS), a platform dedicated to research, exhibitions, and critical discourse on African and diasporic visual arts. Her practice draws on archival research, Black feminist pedagogies, and memory work, with a focus on interdisciplinary and lens-based practices by artists of African descent. She has collaborated with institutions including Guggenheim Abu Dhabi, Serpentine Galleries, Raven Row, and the Barbican, and served on juries for Rencontres de Bamako and BlackStar Film Festival. Her writing has appeared in Third Text, Foam Magazine, and Phaidon, among other publications.

Elisa Medde is an Art Historian specializing in Photography and Visual Culture, focusing on image, communication, and power structures. She has chaired juries for awards like the Luma Rencontres Book Award and MAST Foundation Grant. Elisa collaborates with European universities including ECAL, HSLU, and UWE Bristol. She has curated photobooks and exhibitions, with writings in FlashArt, Time Magazine, Vogue Italia, and more. Editor-in-Chief of Foam Magazine (2012–2023), she won two Lucie Awards and received the 2023 Royal Photographic Society Award for outstanding achievement in Photography Publishing.

Fiona has over 20 years of picture editing experience across newspapers and is a curator, speaker on photojournalism, and mentor in the photography community. She was picture editor of The Guardian for ten years before becoming Head of Photography for Guardian News and Media Group. Fiona covered major historic events like 9/11, global conflicts, natural disasters, and refugee crises. She has judged awards including the Sony World Photography Awards, Taylor Wessing Portrait Prize, and chaired the 2024 World Press Photo Awards jury. Fiona also serves on the board of Stills Gallery, Edinburgh.

Florence Bourgeois has been Director of Paris Photo since 2015. With a background spanning fashion, luxury, and the art world, she previously held positions at Givenchy Parfums, Artcurial, and the Pavillon des Arts et du Design (PAD) in Paris and London. At Paris Photo, she has introduced initiatives including PRISMES, Emergence, and Elles x Paris Photo, developed in partnership with the French Ministry of Culture and Kering’s Women In Motion to increase the visibility and recognition of women artists. She has also overseen the fair’s international expansion in Los Angeles and New York and championed the acquisition of works by women artists through institutional partnerships. Actively involved in the photography ecosystem, she serves on numerous juries and commissions, supporting emerging talent and contemporary photography. In 2023, she was awarded the title of Officière des Arts et des Lettres by the French Minister of Culture.

Florentina Holzinger is an Austrian performance artist and choreographer whose work spans dance, theatre, and opera, exploring the limits of the body through extreme physicality and theatrical experimentation. Her practice challenges the boundaries between high culture and counterculture, spectacle and subversion, often incorporating body modification and a wide range of body-based disciplines. Her productions have received the Nestroy Award for TANZ (2020) and the Faust Award for Ophelia’s Got Talent (2023), and have been selected four times for Theatertreffen Berlin. Since 2021, she has been an associate artist at Volksbühne am Rosa-Luxemburg-Platz in Berlin. In 2026, she represents Austria at the 61st Venice Biennale.

Freelance Writer, Host, Brand Consultant, The Messy Truth Podcast

Gem Fletcher is a writer, consultant and podcaster. Her work has been published in Foam, Aperture, Dazed, Creative Review, 1000 Words and The British Journal of Photography. She also hosts The Messy Truth podcast, a series of candid conversations that unpack the future of visual culture and what it means to be a photographer today.

Ib Kamara is a Sierra Leone-born artist, stylist, and creative director known for his daring, interdisciplinary approach to fashion image-making. Raised in Gambia and educated at Central Saint Martins in London, he served as Editor-in-Chief of Dazed from 2021 to 2025 and Creative Director of Off-White from 2024 to 2026. His work spans editorial and commercial collaborations with artists including Beyoncé, Rihanna, Madonna, and Rosalía, and brands such as Chanel, Louis Vuitton, and Gucci. A contributor to international editions of Vogue, AnOther, and i-D, his work has been exhibited at Somerset House, Red Hook Labs, and the Victoria & Albert Museum. In 2021, he received the British Fashion Council’s Isabella Blow Award for Fashion Creator.

Stylist, Creative Consultant & Fashion Editor

Imruh Asha is a Paris-based stylist, creative consultant, and Fashion Director of Dazed, where he has been part of the team since 2021. Drawing on his Dutch-Caribbean roots and contemporary art, he brings a concept-driven and interdisciplinary approach to fashion image-making. Since his appointment as Fashion Director in 2022, he has pushed the boundaries of fashion imagery through ambitious collaborations, including projects that have broken three official Guinness World Records. In 2021, he presented Future Shock, his first sculpture exhibition, in collaboration with the Ere Foundation at Dover Street Market’s 3537 space.

Jennifer Pastore is an award-winning visual storyteller with more than two decades of experience shaping the imagery of leading magazines and cultural institutions. She is currently the Global Creative Director of Vanity Fair Magazine and previously held roles as the Visuals Director of Sotheby’s Magazine and the Executive Photography Director of WSJ. Magazine, where she commissioned photography, film, and illustration. Earlier in her career, she held roles at Harper’s Bazaar, Teen Vogue, and T: The New York Times Style Magazine. In 2022, she was awarded the Rome Prize in Design by the American Academy in Rome.

Photo Director, Artist & Curator. Former Director of Photography, The New York Times Magazine

Kathy Ryan was the longtime Director of Photography at The New York Times Magazine, where, over 39 years, she pioneered the integration of fine art photography and photojournalism, collaborating with leading photographers and championing new talent. She edited The New York Times Magazine Photographs (Aperture, 2011), which inspired an international touring exhibition, and is the author of Office Romance (Aperture, 2014), a collection of photographs made entirely on her iPhone. Since leaving the Times, she has focused on her own photographic practice, curating exhibitions, teaching at Yale, and speaking internationally. Her numerous accolades include the Royal Photographic Society Award for Outstanding Service to Photography (2012), the International Center of Photography's Spotlight Award (2024), and the Dr. Erich Salomon Prize (2025).

Kira Pollack is a creative director and photo editor pioneering visual storytelling through photography, technology, and digital media. A 2025 Walter Shorenstein Fellow at Harvard Kennedy School, she explores AI’s role in preserving visual history. Formerly Creative Director at Vanity Fair and Director of Photography at TIME, she led iconic projects including The 100 Most Influential Photographs and TIME’s first documentary film unit. Pollack’s work earned Emmy, Lucie, Webby, and National Magazine Awards. She has served as a juror for World Press Photo and Tribeca Film Festival and is based in New York City.

Founder & Creative Director, Be Good Studios

Lina Kutsovskaya is a creative director whose work bridges fashion, art, and advertising. She has led influential campaigns including #MyCalvins at Calvin Klein and creative collaborations with Virgil Abloh at Louis Vuitton. After beginning her career at Vogue, she held creative leadership roles at Nylon, Teen Vogue, Barneys New York, and Calvin Klein, before founding Be Good Studios, a creative agency working across campaigns, brand identity, publishing, and exhibition-making. From 2024 to 2026, she served as Art Director of Another Man, and in 2025 was appointed Contributing Creative Director of Vogue Japan. She is also the founder of Little Big Man, a gallery and publishing project based in Los Angeles.

Melissa Harris is Editor-at-Large at Aperture Foundation, where she served as Editor-in-Chief of Aperture magazine from 2002 to 2012, earning the publication a National Magazine Award for General Excellence. During her more than twenty years at Aperture, she edited over forty photography books and curated exhibitions internationally. Her curatorial projects include Mary Ellen Mark: Encounters (2023–2024), A Kind of Language at Fondazione Prada (2025), and a retrospective of Graciela Iturbide’s work at C/O Berlin (2026). She has taught at Yale, Columbia Journalism School, and New York University, where she has been part of the Tisch School of the Arts for twenty years. She is also Creative Director of Magnum Foundation’s ongoing US Dispatches / Time Capsule project.

Writer, Art Curator & Professor, New York University

Nicole R. Fleetwood is a writer, curator, and professor at New York University, as well as a MacArthur Fellow and elected member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences. She is the author of Marking Time: Art in the Age of Mass Incarceration, which received the 2020 National Book Critics Circle Award, as well as On Racial Icons and Troubling Vision. Her curatorial projects have been presented at institutions including MoMA PS1, Aperture Foundation, the National Underground Railroad Freedom Center, and the Brown Arts Institute. Her work has received support from leading cultural and research institutions, including the Mellon Foundation, Ford Foundation, and New York Public Library’s Cullman Center for Scholars and Writers.

Noelle Théard is a photographer, educator, and the US Head of Photography at The Guardian. Previously, she was Senior Photo Editor at The New Yorker, where she also produced Photo Booth, the magazine’s photography column. Her work focuses on social justice, community engagement, and the intersection of education and visual storytelling. She co-founded FotoKonbit, a nonprofit empowering Haitians to tell their own stories through photography, and has held roles at Magnum Foundation, Parsons, and the Museum of Contemporary Art in Miami. She has also taught African Diaspora and Art History at Florida International University.

Member of the Board of Directors, Friends of Palais de Tokyo

Olivia Anani is a Paris-based curator, writer, and art market expert with a background in Asian Studies and Contemporary Art. She has worked at Christie’s, Sotheby’s, and Phillips, contributing to the sale of major masters and the reevaluation of African artists. Olivia serves on the Board of Friends of Palais de Tokyo and leads its Young Patrons initiative. She supports institutions like the Louvre and is involved in developing a new cultural institution in Benin. Anani has contributed to major monographs and was named among France’s 100 Most Influential Women in Culture in 2021.

Willow Defebaugh is the co-founder and editor-in-chief of Atmos, an award-winning climate and culture magazine that seeks to re-enchant people with our shared humanity and the Earth. She is the author of The Overview, a deep ecology newsletter and book, and host of The Nature Of, a podcast from Atmos. She is a lifelong student of nature and graduated with a degree in creative writing from the University of Michigan. Her work has been featured in Vogue, Harper's Bazaar, Teen Vogue, V Magazine, Interview, i-D, BBC, The Guardian, Them, New York Magazine, and more. She lives in Brooklyn on unceded Lenape territory.

#6580. Extra-Fluffy Cinnamon Rolls

At first glance, these homemade cinnamon rolls have all the classics: buttery, golden-brown dough, a gooey cinnamon-and-brown-sugar filling, and a generous swoop of cream cheese frosting. But a couple of smart moves make them especially fluffy, with a tender crumb that stays soft well into the next day (assuming there are any left).

One is tangzhong, a Chinese technique that cooks a small portion of flour and milk into a thick paste before it’s added to the dough. The precooked starch helps the dough hold on to more moisture, resulting in pillowy, supple cinnamon rolls.

The other is brown butter, which gives the filling a nutty, toasty edge. The tangy cream cheese frosting balances all that richness; add the optional lemon zest for extra brightness.

Can I make these cinnamon rolls the night before?

Yes. You can refrigerate the dough after its first rise or assemble the rolls in their baking pans and refrigerate them before the second rise. Cover tightly with plastic wrap to prevent the dough from drying out. The next day, let the chilled dough sit at room temperature for about an hour before proceeding with the recipe, making sure the shaped rolls have doubled in volume before baking.

This is a soft, moisture-rich dough, but it should become smooth and elastic as you knead it. For the most consistent results, weigh your flour rather than measuring by volume. Also, make sure the tangzhong has thickened into a paste before adding it to the dough: You should be able to see the tracks of your whisk across the bottom of the saucepan. Avoid adding excessive extra flour, which can make the finished rolls dense.

Can I make these cinnamon rolls without a stand mixer?

Yes, though kneading this soft, enriched dough by hand takes considerable time and effort. Several readers have reported success doing so. If using a stand mixer, keep an eye on the motor during the extended kneading time. If it begins to strain or overheat, stop the machine and finish kneading by hand.

Can I use active dry yeast instead of instant yeast?

This recipe calls for instant yeast, which can be mixed directly into the dough. Active dry yeast generally requires activation in warm liquid and may affect rising times, so we recommend sticking with instant yeast for the recipe as written. For more information, see our guide to the different types of yeast.

Watch Zaynab perfect these cinnamon rolls

Save recipes and plan every week with confidence. Download the app

Whisk ¾ cup whole milk and ¼ cup (31 g) all-purpose flour in a medium saucepan until smooth. Place saucepan over medium heat and cook, whisking constantly, until mixture is thickened and whisk lines are visible on bottom of pan, about 2 minutes. Scrape tangzhong into the bowl of a stand mixer and let cool.

Add 1 large egg, one ¼-oz. envelope instant yeast (about 2¼ tsp.), ⅓ cup (67 g) granulated sugar, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt,  and remaining 1½ cups whole milk to tangzhong and whisk to combine. Add remaining 5½ cups (688 g) all-purpose flour. Fit bowl onto stand mixer; fit mixer with dough hook attachment. Mix on low speed until combined, about 1 minute. Increase speed to medium-low and mix, scraping down sides of bowl occasionally, until dough is smooth and elastic, 18–24 minutes. Pinch off a golf-ball-size piece of dough and stretch between your fingers as thin as possible without breaking. If you can see light through the dough, it’s ready. If not, continue mixing a few more minutes, then try again.

Add ½ cup (1 stick) unsalted butter, room temperature, cut into pieces, to dough and mix on medium speed until incorporated, about 2 minutes. Continue mixing until dough pulls away cleanly from sides of bowl and is no longer tacky to the touch, 5–7 minutes longer. Remove bowl from mixer and cover with a damp kitchen towel. Let sit in a warm spot until doubled in volume, 60–90 minutes.

While the dough is rising, cook ½ cup (1 stick) unsalted butter in a small saucepan over medium heat, stirring occasionally, until butter foams and milk solids turn dark amber, about 4 minutes. Transfer to a heatproof bowl and let cool slightly. Add 1 cup (packed; 200 g) dark brown sugar, 2 Tbsp. ground cinnamon, 2 Tbsp. heavy cream, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt to butter and mix to combine.

Butter two 9"-diameter cake pans. Punch down dough and transfer to a lightly floured surface. Stretch dough into a rough rectangle; if dough feels stiff, let sit 5–10 minutes to allow gluten to relax. Arrange dough with short side facing you and roll out to a 24x13" rectangle. Spread filling over dough in an even layer.

Starting at edge closest to you, tightly roll up dough into a log; roll log seam side down. Using a sharp serrated knife and long sawing motions, trim ends of log; discard. Using serrated knife or, preferably, unflavored dental floss, cut log in half crosswise, then cut each half into 6 equal rounds. (If using dental floss, slide floss underneath dough, then cross over top and pull ends through.) Nestle 6 rounds, cut side down, in each prepared cake pan. Cover with damp kitchen towels and let sit in a warm spot until doubled in volume, about 30–50 minutes.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Bake rolls until golden on top and puffed (don’t be alarmed if they rise dramatically in the center), 25–30 minutes.

Meanwhile, using an electric mixer on medium speed or a whisk, beat 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, room temperature, and 8 oz. cream cheese, room temperature, in a large bowl, scraping down sides of bowl as needed, until combined. Add 1¼ cups (138 g) powdered sugar, 1 Tbsp. heavy cream, 1 tsp. lemon zest (if using), and ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt and beat until mixture is smooth and sugar is incorporated. Taste and beat in more powdered sugar (up to ¾ cup) if desired. Thin with more cream as needed, a teaspoonful at a time, until frosting is thick but spreadable.

Let cinnamon rolls cool in pan 5 minutes; spread frosting over.

#6579. A Beautiful Cabbage Galette

Cut this festive galette into little squares for a hearty appetizer, or serve sizeable wedges as a vegetarian main or standout side. It’s worth seeking out savoy cabbage, the ruffly sort that looks like lace. Ordinary green cabbage, which has a higher moisture content and flatter texture, doesn’t work here (we tried).

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Whisk 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, ¼ tsp. baking powder, and 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour in a large bowl. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces, and rub in with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea size). Make a well in the center and pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute. Knead dough in bowl just to bring together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn dough out onto a lightly dusted surface and sprinkle with all-purpose flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting dough with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

When dough is almost done chilling, cut 1 medium head of savoy cabbage (1¾–2¼ lb.) in half and cut out triangular core at bottom; discard. Separate leaves and tear into pieces about the size of your palm. Transfer about half to a large bowl and set aside.

Melt 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add 1 medium white or yellow onion, thinly sliced, and season generously with kosher salt. Cook, stirring occasionally, until softened and starting to turn translucent, about 5 minutes. Add remaining 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter and ¾ tsp. cumin seeds (if using) and cook until butter is melted. Add remaining cabbage leaves and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion is translucent and lightly browned and cabbage is wilted, 18–22 minutes. Transfer to a large plate or a small baking sheet; chill in fridge or freezer until cool.

Place a rack in bottom third of oven; preheat to 400°. Whisk 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, ⅓ cup heavy cream, 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a measuring glass to combine. Pour cream mixture over reserved raw cabbage leaves and toss with your hands to coat. Add 5 oz. Gruyère or sharp cheddar, coarsely grated, and toss again to combine.

Unwrap dough and roll out on a lightly floured sheet of parchment paper to a 13–14" round (some dough will extend beyond the parchment). Transfer on parchment paper to a baking sheet.

Spread cooked cabbage mixture over dough, leaving about a 1½" border around edges. Fold dough up and over filling, folding and tucking as needed to make a rustic border. Pile raw cabbage mixture on top of cooked cabbage mixture to make a dramatic heap. (It will look ridiculously high at first but will cook down when it bakes.)

Bake galette 25 minutes. Rotate baking sheet front to back, reduce heat to 375°, and bake until cabbage and crust are deep golden brown, 25–35 minutes. (If cabbage seems to be browning too much, reduce heat to 350° toward the end.) Let galette cool on baking sheet at least 1 hour and up to 4 hours before serving.

Do Ahead: Sautéed cabbage can be made 1 day ahead. Transfer to an airtight container and chill. Tightly wrap undressed raw cabbage in plastic and chill.

#6575. Bakery Tourism Is Booming—These Are The 15 Spots Everyone Wants To Visit

Your next trip might come with a side of cardamom bun.

Bakeries are no longer just a stop along the way—they’re the final destination. According to Yelp’s 2027 Food and Drink Trend report, bakeries are becoming such a hot commodity that people are planning entire trips around viral treats. Yelp searches for “bakeries near me” are up 561% from last year, while searches for a “sweet treat” are up 303%. Treat yo’ self culture is officially here.

Bakery tourism is on the rise, and honestly, I'm not surprised. I, myself, am prone to walking unfamiliar city streets just to get my hands on the town's most beloved pastry. And people are getting pretty specific about what they want. Searches for cardamom buns are up 24%, kouign-amann 67%, and salt bread a whopping 616%.

It’s not just individual pastries getting all the attention, either. Yelp found that searches for “hot and new bakeries” jumped 359%, while “best gluten-free bakery” rose 113%. Bakeries are also the most-saved type of specialty food shop on Yelp’s My Lists feature. Even New York City's Radio Bakery, which you’ll find below, saw searches increase by 176%. It seems we’re all doing some serious research before our next pastry run.

So which hot spots should you add to your must-visit list? I asked Yelp to do a deep dive into the most-saved bakeries across America to see which ones people are bookmarking. Here's what came out on top.

This famed Taiwanese bakery opened its first U.S. outpost earlier this year in Pasadena, California, and has already gone viral for its unique cream cheese-filled bagels and flaky pastries.

What started out as a pandemic-era creation has now morphed into a line-worthy brick-and-mortar. Bad Butter regularly draws block-long lines, with its breads, croissants, and pastries often selling out.

In Santa Ana, California, 61hundred Bread is known for its signature heirloom blue-corn masa sourdough bread, along with Filipino baked goods like pandesal and ube-filled cruffins.

At this New York City French bakery, the jambon-beurre sandwich is the star item. Fresh baguettes and flaky croissants are also among the other reasons locals and tourists flock to the shop.

Located at the Halepuna Waikiki hotel in Honolulu, Hawaii, Halekulani Bakery is known for its signature coconut cake and assortment of pastries.

Located in Los Angeles, California, Out Of Ordi specializes in Korean-style salt bread.

New York City’s Sunday Morning frequently sells out of its viral cinnamon rolls.

San Diego’s Relic Bakery & Kitchen offers a mix of sweet and savory baked goods, from pies and croissants to breads and danishes.

In New York City, you’ll find Justin’s Salt Bread, voted the city’s best new bakery of the year and known for—you guessed it—its salt bread.

San Francisco’s Butter & Crumble is known for its crumble cakes and laminated pastries, with offerings that rotate seasonally.

Another Honolulu bakery makes the list, although this one comes with a twist. Part bakery, part butcher shop, The Local General Store sells everything from quiche and danishes to sausage and ham.

It looks like my travel schedule just got a little busier (and tastier).

#6574. Gravy-Braised Turkey

Cooking a whole turkey is a commitment. Between the schlepping, trussing, and constant babysitting, it’s a serious investment—and one that doesn’t always pay dividends. For a more laid-back affair, and one that practically guarantees success, might we suggest turkey legs cooked directly in gravy? Yes, in the gravy.

This recipe will defy everything you have probably done to cook a turkey until now. The first important step is searing the whole turkey legs for optimal browning. Now you are ready to create a base for the gravy with all those drippings and toasty bits left in the pot. No need to make a full-on roux either: Just sprinkle in the flour over the melted fat, whisk to combine, and slowly pour in the broth. Once the gravy is done, in goes the turkey and aromatics for braising. The rest is you worrying about something else, because that turkey will cook itself.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Season 4 whole turkey legs (thigh and drumstick; about 6½ lb. total), patted dry, all over with kosher salt and freshly ground pepper. Heat 3 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large braiser or Dutch oven over medium-high. Working in 2 batches if needed to avoid overcrowding, arrange turkey legs, skin side down, in pot and cook, undisturbed, rotating pan on burner a few times to ensure even browning, until browned underneath and they easily release from pot, 8–12 minutes. Transfer turkey legs to a rimmed baking sheet, arranging skin side up. (No need to brown other side; turkey will still be raw at this point.)

Add more oil if pot looks dry; arrange 2 large oranges and/or lemons, halved, and 2 heads of garlic, tops trimmed to expose cloves, cut side down in pot and add 3 large shallots, peeled. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 2–3 minutes. Transfer each to baking sheet with turkey as they are done (it’s okay if some fall apart slightly).

Add 6 Tbsp. (¾ stick) unsalted butter to pot and cook until melted. Sprinkle in ⅓ cup (42 g) all-purpose flour and cook, stirring constantly, until no pockets of dry flour remain, about 1 minute. Gradually pour in 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth, stirring constantly to combine. Bring to a simmer and cook until gravy is just starting to thicken, about 2 minutes. Stir in 3 Tbsp. Worcestershire sauce and season with salt and pepper.

Nestle turkey legs into gravy, skin side up, then tuck oranges, garlic, and shallots around, arranging oranges and garlic cut side up. Add 1 small bunch thyme (about 10 sprigs), tied with kitchen twine, and cover pot tightly with a lid or foil. Braise 2 hours. (If your pot is too small to comfortably fit everything, transfer gravy to a 13x9" baking dish before adding turkey legs and aromatics.) Uncover pot and continue to bake until turkey legs are deeply browned, meat shreds easily off the bone, and gravy has thickened a little, 45–55 minutes.

Let turkey and gravy cool slightly before serving. Transfer to a platter if desired. (If gravy has excess fat on top, skim off with a spoon and discard before serving or spooning over legs on platter.)

#6573. Bon Appétit Pick: HelloFresh Garlicky Shrimp Couscous Bowl

Over the past few years, BA editors have tested—and retested—just about every meal delivery service. Each time we try HelloFresh, we’re impressed by its bold flavors, so we teamed up with the brand to bring you our favorite recipes each week (read more about how we chose them here). Sign up for a delivery, and you also get a 3-month digital subscription to BA for free. Here’s a closer look at one of our BA Picks.

Most nights I try to hit up an exercise class after work, which means when I finally get home in the evening I’m tired, hungry, and craving something full of nutrients. With 26 grams of protein and just 25 minutes of prep-and-cook time, HelloFresh’s Garlicky Shrimp Couscous Bowl is a great solution for dinner.

This flavorful bowl reminds me of Dig Inn’s glory days—only I can enjoy it without elbowing my way through midtown lunchtime mobs. Roasted broccoli and shrimp sautéed with lemon and plenty of garlic are spooned on top of large couscous pearls. Chili flakes add an extra kick.

You’ll need to grab olive oil, butter, salt, and pepper from your own pantry; everything else is included in your delivery. The shrimp arrives fully cleaned and deveined, thank god. I love that a small pouch of veggie stock is included for cooking your couscous, a detail that many meal kits overlook.

True to the recipe card’s promise, the meal cooks in less than half an hour. Prep your mise (chop the broccoli, garlic, and parsley; slice your lemon; rinse the shrimp), then get your broccoli in the oven and couscous on the stove. While they do their thing, you cook the shrimp so that everything finishes around the same time.

I found the instructions incredibly clear to follow, including when to add water and butter to your shrimp, and when to reduce the pan’s heat. I don’t often cook shrimp at home, and I was pleasantly surprised how easy it was and how quickly they pinked up.

In a word: delish! Garlic can cover a multitude of sins, and there’s a generous amount used when cooking both the couscous and shrimp, the latter also includes garlic powder, for good measure. Lemon and parsley give the dish a nice freshness; the flavors remind me of my favorite clam pie from a local Brooklyn pizzeria.

This is a great dish for pescatarians, those looking to cut back on red meat, and health-conscious eaters. The small ingredient list is full of nutritional value: carbs, fats, and lean protein to help me refuel after a long day, plus five grams of fiber and vitamin K, calcium, and potassium from the broccoli (cruciferous veggies are super good for you).

Would make again. Sometimes you want to use your time in the kitchen to discover new flavors and learn new techniques, and sometimes your main goal is getting dinner on the table quickly. This recipe hits on the weeknight trifecta: It’s tasty, easy to make, and nutritious.

#6571. This Jewelry Designer Bride Created Her Own Vintage-Inspired Dress for Her Polish Countryside Wedding

When the Polish jewelry designer Natalia Kopiszka was planning her August 2026 wedding to actor Aleksander “Olek” Kaleta, she found herself at a bridal fashion crossroads, stuck between two stylistic pillars of her own brand: vintage and modern.

First, the Warsaw-based designer of Kopi traveled to Paris to shop for a vintage wedding dress, but returned home empty-handed. “I didn’t find anything that I liked, so I thought: I will design my own wedding dress,” Natalia says.

For the body of her ceremony dress, she ordered fabric—silk taffeta—from Etsy. “I was on a mission to find the absolute dream silk fabric,” she says. “I started by checking out local fabric shops and silk wholesalers, but I just couldn't find the right silk taffeta with that delicate, subtle sheen anywhere.” She searched online and stumbled upon a listing from a New York-based seller, which she ordered on the spot. Luckily, “it turned out to be even more breathtaking in person than in the photos,” she says.

Then, on a weekend trip to Amsterdam with a friend, she wandered into a vintage store where she found antique lace, which she used for the bodice detailing. “The lace is truly unique because it dates back to the early 20th century, and I only had a tiny piece of it—which happened to be just enough to trim the bodice,” Natalia says. “It was such a special way to check off the ‘something old’ tradition.” She sketched the dress, then shared her designs with a dressmaker who sewed it, making her vintage-modern dream a reality.

Natalia and Olek first met in February 2021 at a house party in Warsaw. “For me, it was love at first sight,” Natalia recalls. “A friend of mine who lived in the apartment below me threw a get-together, and her roommate happened to be friends with Olek. As soon as he walked in, we instantly locked eyes. I’m pretty sure he was the one who came over and started the conversation first,” she adds. “It also turned out that Olek lived directly across the street from my apartment, so we used to wave at each other from our windows. Ever since that night, we started seeing each other almost every single day.”

After a year, they moved in together in Warsaw. In 2024, Olek proposed to Natalia during a trip to Italy, in the coastal town of Polignano a Mare. “It was a warm, romantic evening with a huge moon, and surprisingly, I didn't see it coming at all,” Natalia says. “It turned out to be such a sweet, funny moment because neither of us could stop laughing.”

On August 8, 2026, the couple held their wedding at Pałac Pstrokonie, a historic 19th-century palace in a small village outside of Warsaw. They worked with the wedding planner Kasia Fastyn, who brought Natalia’s vision—a romantic, whimsical wonderland of sorts—to life, pairing them with the event studio MyBigDay, who designed the florals and draped their dancing tent in pink fabric.

As a jewelry and accessories designer, Natalia zeroed in on all the details of her wedding looks from the beginning. She knew she didn’t want a traditional floral bouquet, for example, so she opted for a small silk bag in the shape of a bouquet from the New York-based designer Camille Albertine, after finding her work on Instagram. Albertine custom-made Natalia’s bouquet purse in the same fabric as her dress. “Everyone was so surprised that I didn’t have a typical bouquet,” Natalia says. “It’s versatile enough that I can wear it with everyday outfits. It’s going to stay with me for a long time, and I’ll even be able to pass it down through generations.”

For her reception look, the bride changed into a dress by the Polish designer Magda Butrym, pairing it with an unexpected accessory: a crochet veil cap that her sister made. “It was a really simple dress, also silk, but I put something really crazy on my head,” Natalia says.

Natalia incorporated her own jewelry into the crochet cap-like veil, which was bedazzled with charms and pendants. “They are specially made charms with little lobster clasps so you can clip them onto the crochet work however you like. They’re gold-plated and feature Swarovski crystals,” Natalia says. (Charms are a signature of Natalia’s brand, she explains, so it was only fitting to work them into her bridal looks.) Her love of historical pieces, particularly from the Victorian era, inspired the final design, which included blue stones for her “something blue.” A look inspired by it is now for sale as part of Kopi’s “I Do” bridal line.

The bride also made Olek a pocket square with the same vintage lace as her dress, so they were matching (and so he had “something old” as well). They completed their looks with wedding bands that Natalia designed. “Mine has a retro feel, crafted in gold and set with 12 small diamonds,” she says of the rings. “Olek went for a classic look—a simple, wide gold band with my nickname engraved on the inside.” Reflecting on the wedding months later, Natalia says: “Everything was perfect.”

#6568. Buttered Nut Squash

We rate butternut the most affable winter squash—relatively easy to prepare, consistently delicious, and available at most grocery stores. The buttered nut dressing is more than just cheeky wordplay. Bold from brown butter and balsamic vinegar and bright from lemon, the crunchy topping is an excellent foil to the sweetness of roasted squash. Cook the squash a couple hours ahead of time and all you’ll have left to do before dinner is make the dressing.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in lower third of oven; preheat to 425°. Lightly crush 2 tsp. fennel seeds with a mortar and pestle or place on a cutting board and gently crush with a heavy pan. Peel 1 medium butternut squash (about 3 lb.) and halve lengthwise. Scoop out seeds; discard. Cut squash into 2" irregular pieces, aiming for sharp, jagged shapes. Transfer to a large rimmed baking sheet; drizzle with 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil and sprinkle with fennel seeds, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. crushed red pepper flakes. Toss squash to coat, arrange in a single layer, and roast until browned and tender, 30–35 minutes.

Do Ahead: Squash can be roasted 2 hours ahead. Store at room temperature.

While the squash is roasting, cook 6 oz. thick-cut bacon, cut into 1" pieces, in a medium skillet over medium heat, stirring often, until browned and mostly crisp, 8–12 minutes. Transfer to a small plate with a slotted spoon.

Reduce heat to low; combine 1 cup raw pecans and 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter in same pan. Cook, stirring often, until butter browns and nuts have slightly darkened, 6–8 minutes. Remove from heat. Stir in 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped (this will give it a head start to take off the raw edge), then add bacon, zest and juice of 1 large lemon, 3 sprigs sage, and 2 Tbsp. balsamic vinegar and stir to combine. Taste dressing and season with kosher salt if needed.

Arrange squash on a platter and spoon dressing over.

#6564. In Alison Roman's World, Curation is King

With only weeks before opening, Alison Roman’s Brooklyn brick-and-mortar is still unfinished. “Today they’re doing up the walls and putting in the floors,” Roman says. In short, it does not yet look like a dreamy European-inspired grocer. There are still a mountain of calls to be made, meetings to be had, speed bumps to overcome.

The chaos doesn’t seem to be getting to the cookbook author, chef, and aspiring empire-builder. “It’s been so fun,” Roman, a Bon Appétit alum, says of the process. Perhaps that shouldn’t be a surprise; this breezy effortlessness is at the bedrock of the Alison Roman universe. You know the kind of nonchalant magic I’m talking about: chilling wine bottles in a bathtub of ice, buckets of take-out fried chicken at dinner parties—I mean, this woman was one of the foremost proponents of brothy beans.

What Roman has built has grown beyond recipes and bean propaganda. The ever-creeping edges of her lifestyle brand now encompass a jarred tomato sauce brand, once cheekily titled A Very Good Sauce, now renamed Roman’s. There’s also the new podcast, Having People Over, where she hosts guests for a meal and a yap, plus the speaking tour she’s calling “Food, Life and Other Strong Opinions.” There are the shoes (sleek mules and chunky clogs) she made in collaboration with New York–based footwear brand Margaux. And now First Bloom, the grocery store–slash–wine bar–slash–café that—as of mid-November—is on track to open in December.

The Brooklyn shop is an extension of the original Catskill’s location of the same name. Roman says this new outpost is “a totally different proposition of what we are offering people.” There’s more budget to work with, there’s more staff, there’s more space, and there’s more food.

Whereas the upstate location’s function is closer to utility—meat and produce from local farms are a major feature—in Brooklyn (where specialty grocers abound) Roman is focusing on something more akin to world-building. But do not call First Bloom a shoppy shop, those whimsically designed boutiques that seem to pop up everywhere selling the same $45 squiggly candlesticks and squeeze-bottle olive oils everyone seems to have. “I think ‘shoppy shop’ is derogatory,” Roman says. “In a world where you can buy anything from anywhere, sometimes it’s nice to be told what to do.”

At Brooklyn’s First Bloom, the shelves will be stocked with products that Roman herself deems “hyper-defensible.” There’s a reason they’re stocked, and a reason for how they’re priced. They’re best in class or a personal favorite of Roman’s. “Perspective and curation is a really special thing to be able to convey,” she says.

The vision for First Bloom is set, but with the opening just a month out, Roman doesn’t have all the details nailed down. “We are going to have a rotisserie chicken,” she says. “I don’t know how much it’s going to cost yet,” she follows up quickly, before I can ask. There will also be a couple salads and a couple sandwiches on offer—plus another secret off-menu sandwich for the neighborhood regulars and the real Roman-heads who know to ask for it. “I’m very if-you-know-you know,’” she says. But Brooklyn’s First Bloom isn’t just for popping into—you’ll be able to lounge with a glass of wine or relax with a snack and a coffee.

Alison Roman’s world is organic, craft-centered, and easy but considered. To step into it is an enticing foil to the AI-fueled tasteslop tilt-a-whirl on which we find ourselves. It’s a vision of a slow, steady, wabi-sabi life that many of us only aspire to. A life where one can even somehow enjoy, say, a monthslong commercial renovation project in one of America’s most competitive real estate markets. That’s the draw of First Bloom. The hard-to-find tinned fish, yes, but also the ease of living in Alison’s world if only for an hour.

And if not, well, it seems like there’ll be a pretty good rotisserie chicken, at least.

#6562. Kim and Khloé Kardashian’s Beauty Trip Didn’t Quite Go to Plan—Here’s What to Know Before Booking Yours

Between the salmon sperm facials, the skin boosters, and the next generation of lasers, there’s plenty to pique the interest of the beauty obsessive in South Korea. So much so that vacations are increasingly being organized around visits to the dermatologist’s office. But how much is too much when it comes to our beauty itineraries? Just ask Khloé and Kim Kardashian.

On Wednesday’s episode of her podcast, Khloé in Wonder Land, Koko and her close friend La La Anthony reminisced about their August 2025 trip to South Korea, where they enthusiastically availed themselves of the country’s advanced cosmetic treatments—with some less-than-desirable results.

“Kim and I came back deformed, you came back beautiful and the plane ride just made it so much worse,” Kardashian told Anthony, recalling how their post-treatment appearances had kept them holed up in their hotel room.

The Kardashians are, of course, well-versed in the world of aesthetics. Over the years, the sisters have been particularly candid about their experiments with everything from the vampire facial to regenerative skin treatments. But even for those with the world’s most sought-after dermatologists on speed dial, things don’t always go to plan.

While it’s unclear precisely which procedures the sisters underwent—photos shared on Kim’s Instagram at the time showed her receiving facial treatments and an IV infusion—their experience raises some pertinent questions. How much research should we be doing before traveling abroad for cosmetic treatments? How many procedures can we feasibly—and safely—fit into a vacation? And how do we know when something has actually gone wrong?

The lure of a beauty vacation is understandable. South Korea, in particular, is at the forefront of aesthetic innovation, with technologies and treatments that aren’t yet widely available in the United States. And as our collective beauty literacy has expanded, so too has our appetite for more technologically sophisticated treatments. A facial no longer necessarily means an hour of extractions and massage. But there is a distinction to be made between a beauty treatment and a medical procedure. Just because something is marketed as minimally invasive, or requires no incisions, doesn’t mean it is without risk. Nor does its ubiquity on TikTok necessarily speak to its suitability for your own skin.

“Traveling for treatment isn't the same as having unsafe treatment,” says consultant dermatologist Dr. Sidra Khan. “What travel adds is complexity: a different regulatory system, possibly a language barrier, often a compressed consultation, and being thousands of miles from your practitioner during recovery.”

“A beautiful clinic, an impressive Instagram following and a gallery of celebrity clients don’t really tell you much about the practitioner’s medical credentials or what results you might expect,” adds cosmetic surgeon and aesthetics specialist Dr. Paul Banwell. Independently verify your practitioner’s qualifications and registration with the relevant medical regulator, and establish whether the clinic is equipped to manage complications. Khan recommends arranging a virtual consultation with the treating doctor before booking anything, and asking about their experience with your particular skin tone, the products and devices they intend to use, and why. “A holiday itinerary shouldn't replace informed consent.”

For London-based aesthetics and NHS doctor Dr. Alicia Gonzalez-Fernandez, the marketing of medical procedures as vacation packages is itself a red flag. “On a handful of occasions, I have encountered patients that have come into A&E straight from the airport,” she says of her experiences working in emergency medicine. She cautions against practitioners who pressure patients into additional procedures or fail to adequately discuss complications and aftercare. “We are not in the business of making people self-conscious about things that are not a problem for them.”

Then there’s the phenomenon of “treatment stacking.” While certain procedures can complement one another, squeezing several into a short period of time can increase the likelihood of complications. “Many of these treatments work by creating a controlled injury that the skin then repairs, and doing several close together doesn't give it time to recover,” explains aesthetics doctor Dr. Priya Verma. “That raises the risk of prolonged inflammation, infection and pigmentation changes, particularly in darker skin tones.”

Multiple procedures can also make it harder to establish which treatment is responsible for an adverse reaction, notes aesthetics doctor Dr. Ahmed El Muntasar. “Ultimately, I’d much rather a patient’s treatment schedule was dictated by how their skin is recovering than by the date of their flight home.”

Consider, too, how conducive the rest of your vacation itinerary is to your skin’s recovery. As Verma notes, the low humidity in airplane cabins can exacerbate dryness and sensitivity in already compromised skin, while sun exposure can increase the risk of post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation. There is no universal rule about how soon you can fly after a non-surgical cosmetic procedure, says Khan, but you should allow ample time for recovery and an in-person review before your departure. (With surgical procedures, flying also carries an increased risk of blood clots, making a conversation with your surgeon about your travel plans particularly important.)

There's also the question of downtime. An unfortunate-looking reflection in the hotel bathroom mirror doesn’t necessarily mean a treatment has been “botched.” Verma makes an important distinction: “Downtime is the expected redness, swelling or flaking that settles over a few days. Dissatisfaction is when the skin has healed but you're not happy with the result. A complication is a medical problem that needs treating.”

Knowing what to expect—and for how long—is something to establish with your practitioner well before the treatment itself. The trajectory of your recovery is key: Increasing pain, spreading redness, heat, discharge, or fever warrant prompt medical attention.

There are, however, symptoms that warrant immediate medical attention. Following dermal filler injections, for example, the FDA advises seeking immediate medical care for unusual pain, changes to your vision, white, gray, or blue discoloration around the injection site, or signs of a stroke. These may indicate that the blood supply has been compromised.

“If there are red-flag symptoms, don't just get on a plane because you'd rather deal with it at home,” stresses Khan. “Some complications are time-critical, so get seen locally.”

In non-emergency situations, contact your original practitioner for an in-person review and document your recovery with photographs taken in consistent lighting. El Muntasar recommends obtaining your full treatment records, including the names, quantities, and batch numbers of any injectables, or the device and settings used for laser treatments. Seek an independent medical opinion from someone experienced in managing complications if you remain concerned.

As distressing as it can be to feel unhappy with your appearance, resist the temptation to immediately book another aesthetic procedure. “Swelling can make certain areas appear overfilled or disproportionate, and adding more filler to try to balance things out can leave a patient with an entirely different problem once that swelling subsides,” explains Banwell.

“More treatment isn’t always the antidote to treatment,” says Khan. Anti-wrinkle injections can take around two weeks to reach their full effect, filler can take several weeks to settle, and collagen remodeling following laser treatments or microneedling continues for months. The same caution applies to overzealous at-home skincare. “Your freshly lasered face is not the moment to try the acids and retinoids you picked up at duty-free.”

And while you might have meticulously mapped out your Seoul shopping itinerary, restaurant reservations, and dermatology appointments, have you given quite as much thought to what happens when you get home? Establishing a plan for follow-up care, obtaining a record of your procedures, and checking whether your insurance covers complications should all factor into the planning process. El Muntasar recommends getting your aftercare plan in writing, including details of who you can contact outside of clinic hours and who is responsible for any additional medical expenses should you need to extend your stay.

By all means, indulge your K-beauty curiosity. Just make sure you’re approaching your dermatological appointments with a little more discernment than your haul at Olive Young.

#6561. Collard Greens Vinaigrette

For those who might shudder at the thought of eating raw hardy greens like collards or kale, this vibrant side inspired by the French bistro classic leeks vinaigrette is the answer. Simmered past squeaky-raw yet well short of meltingly braised, they offer substantial bite, like al dente pasta. The mustard dressing couldn’t be simpler to make—use it as a base for any salad you might serve this season. It’s punchy enough to stand up to winter vegetables or any sturdy bitter green.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Toast ½ cup raw walnuts on a rimmed baking sheet, tossing halfway through, until golden brown, 10–12 minutes.

Meanwhile, cook 2 bunches collard greens, ribs and stems removed, leaves cut into 2" pieces, in a large pot of generously salted boiling water until just tender, 9–11 minutes. Using tongs, immediately transfer to a large bowl of ice water and let cool.

Whisk 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, ¼ cup white wine vinegar, 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, preferably country-style, ⅓ cup extra-virgin olive oil, ¼ cup (packed) coarsely chopped tarragon, 2 tsp. sugar, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl to combine. Set dressing aside.

Transfer toasted walnuts to a small bowl and drizzle with remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Sprinkle with a generous pinch each of sugar and salt and toss to coat. Taste and add more sugar if needed (nuts should be more sweet than salty). Set seasoned walnuts aside.

Drain collard greens and squeeze gently to remove excess water. Transfer to bowl with reserved dressing and toss to coat evenly. Cover and chill at least 15 minutes and up to 2 hours.

Arrange greens in a shallow bowl or on a platter and spoon any dressing remaining in bowl over. Top with seasoned walnuts and tarragon leaves.

Do Ahead: Walnuts can be toasted and dressing can be made 1 day ahead. Store walnuts airtight at room temperature. Cover dressing and chill.

#6556. The Art of Being Veruschka: Fashion Pays Tribute to a Legend

“There is and will always be only one Veruschka,” Richard Avedon wrote in the May 1972 issue of Vogue in an impassioned tribute to his muse. More than half a century later, his words still ring true. Since news broke of the German supermodel’s death at the age of 87, generations of fashion’s image-makers, designers, and models have been reflecting on her immeasurable influence.

A protagonist of some of the most fantastical fashion editorials ever committed to the pages of Vogue and a prolific cover star, Veruschka helped expand the possibilities of what a model could be. Her body was her artistic medium, her imagination as instrumental to the making of a photograph as that of the person behind the lens. Her creative curiosity would endure long after her heyday in the 1960s and ’70s, finding expression in her experiments with body painting and camouflage, her performance art, and her occasional, much-feted returns to the runway.

For those who knew and worked with Veruschka, though, there was as much to marvel at away from the camera: her generosity of spirit, quiet eccentricities, intellectual curiosity, and her sense of humor. In the tributes shared with Vogue below, fellow models recall their first encounters with a woman whose photographs once adorned their bedroom walls, while designers and photographers reflect on the creative communion they shared with her—and how rare a model like Veruschka is today.

I am so sad to hear the news of Veruschka’s passing. When I started modeling in 1966, she was one of my idols—she was so beautiful and exotic. I had always wanted to meet her, and then in the 1980s, while I was appearing on Broadway in the musical My One and Only, a knock came on my dressing room door after the performance. I opened it and, to my surprise and huge delight, Veruschka was standing there. It was so lovely to finally meet her, and she was absolutely divine, and we chatted for ages. She certainly is one of the greatest of all models. RIP, beautiful lady.

Veruschka was an extraordinary artist that I was blessed to know. Thank you, Vera…

I remember sitting in the library at Saint Martins, transfixed by the camouflage photographs in Veruschka: Trans-Figurations, the book she made with Holger Trülzsch. Years later, when I had the chance to work with her, I knew I wanted her to close my spring/summer 2011 show. We flew her in from Berlin and made her a bespoke dress for the finale. What I loved about working with her was how open she was to the ideas behind the collection and how wholeheartedly she embraced them. She was 71 and absolutely majestic on the runway. She had a presence unlike anyone else. A creative powerhouse and a true original.

Being a model is an art form, and she was one of the people who truly mastered it. She had both creativity and respect for what she was doing. When we worked with her, she was incredibly impressive. There was an energy, a grace, and a lasting presence that you don’t see so often today. The lifespan of a model’s career seems to have become so much shorter. I sometimes wonder if, in the way the industry works today, we’re leaving less room for someone to become truly iconic.

When I was a young girl, my bedroom walls were covered in photographs of Veruschka. To me, she looked like she had stepped out of another world—a dream I looked up to, one of the incredible women who had paved the way before me. I used to lie in bed, staring at those pictures, wondering what it would be like actually to know someone like her. Years later, that dream literally knocked on my door.

We ended up living together at our agent Zoli’s house on East 63rd Street. For months, after a long day’s work, we would settle in for the evening with our sketchbooks. I can still see her drawing her little cats—curled up, stretching out, or peeking from the corners of the pages—while I sketched beside her. We didn’t need to say much; the quiet between us always felt so full.

Veruschka was always an enigma to me, a woman with a poetic soul and a nature I could never quite put a name to. She had a wicked little smile and a twinkle in her eye when she’d look up from her drawing, as if she knew a secret about the world she might someday share. Her voice was low and sensuous, and she was always kinder than anyone needed to be.

Sometimes, while watching her sketch, I would think back to that little girl staring at the pictures on her wall. I wished I could tell her that one day she would be sitting right beside her icon, and that Veruschka would be her friend. I have always loved Veruschka, and I always will. Knowing she taught me that dreams really do come true. She was mine.

#6555. Thanksgiving Cornbread

Traditionally, cornbread stuffing requires making cornbread, cubing it and letting it dry out, mixing it with stock, eggs, meat, and aromatics, then transforming it into a stuffing (or dressing). This process produces some truly memorable casseroles, but I have an alternative that streamlines the process without compromising flavor: stuffing cornbread. It still smells enticingly like the classic Thanksgiving side as you set the baking dish on the table. I’ve still packed in a medley of woodsy herbs, sweet onions, vegetal peppers, and savory sausage. And it still slices into lofty servings to perch on your plate next to the sweet potatoes and green beans. It just takes half as long to make.

The intentional two-to-one ratio of cornmeal to flour in this cornbread results in a moist, tender crumb that still has enough structure to hold up against the sturdy mix-ins. The sugar might seem like a lot, but it balances out the savory sausage and aromatics perfectly.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 400°. Line a 13x9" baking pan with parchment paper, leaving generous overhang on long sides. Coat pan and parchment with unsalted butter. Melt ½ cup (1 stick) unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium-low heat, then pour into a small bowl.

Cook 1 green bell pepper, halved, ribs and seeds removed, finely chopped, 1 medium white onion, finely chopped, and 2 celery stalks, finely chopped, in same skillet, stirring occasionally with a wooden spoon, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 1 lb. spicy and/or sweet Italian sausage, casings removed, and cook, breaking up and stirring occasionally, until browned (it may still be a little raw in the center at this point), about 5 minutes. Remove from heat.

Stir together 4 cups (624 g) fine-ground yellow cornmeal, 2 cups (250 g) all-purpose flour, 1 cup (200 g) sugar, 1 Tbsp. plus 1½ tsp. baking powder, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 tsp. baking soda, and ¼ cup finely chopped sage, thyme, and/or rosemary in a large bowl. Gradually pour in 3½ cups buttermilk, then melted butter, stirring constantly until combined. Add 4 large eggs one at a time, mixing to incorporate after each addition. Fold in sausage mixture, then scrape batter into prepared pan.

Bake cornbread, rotating pan front to back halfway through, until golden brown and top springs back when gently pressed, 38–45 minutes. Let cool in pan 15 minutes. Using parchment paper overhang, lift cornbread out of pan and transfer to a cutting board. Cut into 12–18 slices; arrange on a platter.

Do Ahead: Cornbread can be baked 4 hours ahead. Store at room temperature; cut just before serving.

#6553. Brown Butter Sage Chicken Skillet

Boasting a brief ingredient list and a short cooking time, this easy chicken dish is one you’ll be making all season. Basic butter becomes the star here—it turns brown and nutty, then gets infused with sage and garlic for a savory sauce that’s basted over simply seasoned chicken breasts. A big squeeze of lemon, plus its zest, helps balance the richness. This skillet dinner is perfect for a speedy weeknight meal, but it’s also special enough for company.

The protein:You don’t have to limit yourself to chicken here. Feel free to replace the breasts with pork chops, shrimp, scallops, or skinless salmon or halibut fillets. Simply adjust the cooking time to properly cook the protein, but be sure to maintain a medium heat. While meat and fish are often cooked on medium-high heat for a nice char, it needs to be a bit lower to avoid bitter residue in the pan, since the butter will be browned immediately afterward.

The crunch:The sage leaves crisp while the butter browns, but there are also ways to add more texture. Stirring in a handful of slivered almonds toward the end of cooking adds to the nuttiness of the dish; pine nuts, pistachios, or roughly chopped walnuts would also work. If you have a container of them, feel free to sprinkle some fried onions on top tableside.

Storage and serving ideas:This is not a make-ahead situation; it should be eaten immediately after it’s cooked. Serve with a simple salad dressed in a light vinaigrette to balance the richness. To soak up the sauce, mashed potatoes—traditional or sweet—are ideal. Or, to add another nutty element, roast some Brussels sprouts, cauliflower, or butternut squash to eat alongside and round out the meal.
